name: Elena Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive for my uncle's haulage firm, six trucks, family name on the doors. Most days I'm taking pallets for local factories, a furniture maker, a packaging plant, a brewery, out to their customers and the big distribution centres. I like that it's ours and that customers know us by name. What wears me out is that I'm the new one, so I get the awkward runs, and I still take two goes at most loading bays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do besides driving?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In the evenings I help my uncle with the office side, because he hates computers. I use AI every day for quotes, invoices, planning loads, even checking the rules on driving hours. I've got a good bit saved and a small share in the firm he gave me when I started, and my partner Lukas works on his family's farm, so we're comfortable. My uncle wants me to take over one day, and I want that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools I use are still handy, and the business carries on. I'd probably post something on the firm's page about being a proper family haulier. At the yard my uncle would say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan works. I learn the driving properly, I take on more of the office, and in ten years I run the firm. The worries are the usual ones, diesel prices, the big hauliers undercutting us, and whether I'm good enough behind the wheel yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep using AI to speed up quotes, which already saves us hours a week. I'd talk my uncle into a proper booking system. And I'd put some of my savings into a seventh truck in a year or two if work keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI already saves hours. Give me an example.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer emails at nine at night wanting a price for twelve pallets to the coast. I put the details in, the AI drafts a quote with our rates, I check it and send it before bed. My uncle used to do that on paper the next morning, and sometimes we'd lost the job by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a seventh truck, rather than keeping things as they are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a family firm that doesn't grow slowly shrinks. My grandfather started with one truck and a lot of nerve. I want to add to what he built, not just keep it ticking over.

I'd post about being a proper **family haulier** on the firm's page.
think: My plan works: learn to drive well, take on the office, and **run the firm**.
My worries are **diesel prices** and big hauliers **undercutting** us.
do: Use **AI** to speed up quotes, saving hours a week.
Persuade my uncle to adopt a proper **booking system**.
Put savings toward a **seventh truck** in a year or two.

fieldNote: She mixes **family tradition** with heavy, everyday use of AI.

Her wish to **invest** in growth stands out for a junior driver.

steps.text: Draft every evening quote with AI using the firm's rates
Put savings toward a seventh truck within two years
Keep driving the factory pallet runs to learn the trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small firms that move fast. We can do with AI what used to need a whole office. I'd say it online and to other small hauliers I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps us more than it hurts. The office work my uncle hates gets done by software, and I can drive more. The danger is the big hauliers using it to cut prices even harder, so we have to be quicker than them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in a proper AI booking and planning system this year, maybe a few hundred a month. I'd train my uncle on the basics, gently. I'd keep driving, and I'd start learning about the driver-assist trucks, so we know when it's worth buying one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your uncle take the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble for a month and then pretend it was his idea. He's sixty-one and he's done everything on paper and the phone since the eighties. But he trusts me, and he knows the paperwork is killing him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone at the firm worse off in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our part-time bookkeeper, Margit, maybe. If the software does the invoices, she's got less to do. I'd want to find her something else, like chasing new customers, because she knows everyone in town.

I'd say AI does what used to need **a whole office**.

fieldNote: She sees AI as a way for a **small firm** to compete with big hauliers.

steps.text: Bring in an AI booking and planning system this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge chance for anyone ready, but too fast for most families and small firms. I wouldn't ask for handouts, but I'd want the rules to stop big companies using it to crush small ones. I'd say that to our local business group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one frightens me for the firm, not for me. By 2031 the big hauliers will have robot trucks that run all night with no wages, and we've got six trucks with drivers. My uncle's whole life could be worth nothing in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with my uncle and plan how we'd buy our first self-driving truck the moment they're legal. I'd stop the seventh-truck plan and keep the cash ready. I'd also look at the jobs robots can't do yet, like the furniture maker's deliveries where you need to carry and set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but mostly anxious for my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking work changes in 2028 and the robots come about three years later. What do you do in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those three years I'd automate everything in the office, quotes, planning, invoices, so we're as cheap as we can be. Then by 2031 I'd want money in the bank to buy robot trucks, not just watch the big firms buy them. It's a race, and I'd rather run it than stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the drivers at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. There are five drivers besides me, and two of them have been with my uncle twenty years. I'd want to keep them on for the work that needs hands, the set-ups and difficult drops, as long as it lasts.

I'd want rules to stop **big companies** crushing small ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a small firm to get ready if it's smart. I'd tell other family hauliers to start now. I'd say the government should keep out of the way except to stop the big firms cheating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd make it, just about. The office goes digital by 2031, and robot trucks come around 2034. That's time to save, learn and buy at the right moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in the AI office system now and still buy the seventh truck, but a used one, cheap. Around year three I'd start saving hard for robot trucks. I'd train our older drivers in the set-up and installation work some customers want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a determined way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your uncle agree with all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. My uncle would say we're a driving firm and always will be, but he's stubborn, not stupid. He'd come round when the big hauliers start winning our contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm didn't make it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine personally, I've got savings and I'm young. I'd probably go and work for whoever runs the robot fleets, because I know the customers and the routes. But I'd feel I let my family down.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for a smart small firm to **get ready**.
I'd say government should only step in to stop **big firms cheating**.
think: We'd **make it**, just about, with time to save and learn.
Robot trucks around **2034** give time to **buy** at the right moment.
do: Bring in the **AI office** system now and buy a cheap **used truck**.
Start saving hard for **robot trucks** in year three.
Train older drivers in **set-up work** customers want.
S3.quote: My uncle would say we're a driving firm and always will be, but he's stubborn, not stupid.
fieldNote: She has a **staged plan**: digital office now, robot trucks later.
Her personal safety net is strong, but **family pride** is at stake.
She'd retrain **older drivers** rather than let them go.

steps.text: Bring in the AI office system for quotes and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who works hard and plans. Small firms have time to adapt, so there's no excuse. I'd say it at the business group and on the firm's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm calm about this one. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and probably running the firm, with time to plan exactly when to switch to robot trucks. My uncle would be retired by then, so it'd be my decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the firm steadily, add the seventh truck, and keep using AI in the office. Around 2034 I'd start buying the first self-driving trucks as they become reliable. I'd keep the drivers on for the hands-on work as long as customers want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the decade that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy, maybe, thinking we've got loads of time. And the big firms will have ten years too, so it's not like we get a head start. We'd have to stay sharp the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the firm to look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want our family name still on the truck doors, even if the trucks drive themselves. A few people doing the bits robots can't, like the careful deliveries and talking to customers. And me in the office, using AI like I do now, just more of it.

I'd say small firms have time to adapt, so there's **no excuse**.
think: I'd likely be **running the firm** by 2039.
I'd have time to choose when to switch to **robot trucks**.
do: Grow the firm and add the **seventh truck**.
Start buying **self-driving trucks** around 2034 as they become reliable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big hauliers would have robot trucks before a family firm like ours could afford them. What would help is fair rules so small firms can buy into the new trucks too, maybe loans for small businesses, and customers who value a firm that knows them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. The furniture maker has used us for thirty years because my uncle answers the phone at ten at night. I want to keep that, whatever drives the trucks.
